name: Blood, fish and bone
for: A balanced feed for almost anything: vegetables, fruit, roses and borders.
how: Scatter it over the soil and rake or fork it in lightly, then water. It works over a few weeks as the soil breaks it down.
when: A week or two before sowing or planting, and round fruit, roses and shrubs in early spring.
dose: a good handful a square metre
careful: Dogs and foxes like the smell. Fork it in, and keep the box shut.

name: Chicken manure pellets
for: Leafy crops and hungry ones: brassicas, leeks, potatoes and sweetcorn.
how: Scatter and fork them in before planting, or sprinkle round growing plants and water them in.
when: Spring and early summer. Rich in nitrogen, so not for crops you want to stop growing leaves.
dose: a handful and a half a square metre
careful: Wear gloves, and wash your hands after.

name: Liquid seaweed
for: A tonic rather than a full meal: trace elements for seedlings, pots, herbs and anything looking peaky.
how: Dilute it in a can of water, as the bottle says, and water it round the roots or over the leaves.
when: Every two weeks or so from late spring to late summer.
dose: a capful in a can of water

name: Bonemeal
for: Roots getting going: trees, shrubs, fruit bushes and bulbs at planting.
how: Mix a sprinkle into the planting hole, or into the soil you fill it with.
when: At planting, any time of year. It works slowly, over months.
dose: a small handful in the hole
careful: Dogs dig for it. Mix it in well.

name: Garden compost
for: Feeding the soil itself: it holds water, feeds the worms and opens up clay.
how: Spread it as a mulch, 5 cm deep, round plants or over a bed, or dig it into a planting hole.
when: Autumn and spring, on damp soil. Any time in a planting hole.
homeMade: Made in a compost bin from kitchen peelings and garden waste: free.

name: Well-rotted manure
for: Hungry crops and fruit: squashes, potatoes, beans, leeks, roses and rhubarb.
how: Dig it in before planting, or spread it as a mulch round fruit and roses, clear of the stems.
when: Autumn or late winter, a few weeks before planting.
careful: Only when it's dark, crumbly and doesn't smell. Fresh manure scorches roots, and carrots fork in it.

name: Comfrey tea
for: Fruit and flowers: tomatoes, beans, courgettes and anything in flower. High in potash.
how: Dilute it about one part to ten of water, the colour of weak tea, and water it round the roots.
when: Every week or two once the first flowers open.
homeMade: Pack comfrey leaves in a bucket, weigh them down, top up with water and leave for four to six weeks. It smells: keep a lid on. Free.

name: Nettle tea
for: Leafy crops: cabbages, kale, chard, lettuce and leeks. High in nitrogen.
how: Dilute it about one part to ten of water and water it round the roots.
when: Every two weeks while leafy crops are growing, spring to late summer.
homeMade: Young nettles, in gloves, in a bucket of water with a lid, for two to three weeks. Free.

name: Liquid tomato feed
for: Anything fruiting or flowering: tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, courgettes, strawberries, and pots of flowers. High in potash.
how: Dilute it in a can of water, as the bottle says, and water it round the roots on damp compost.
when: Every week or two from the first flowers to the end of summer.
dose: as the bottle says, in a can of water
careful: Both organic and mineral kinds are sold, and work the same. Too strong scorches roots.

name: Balanced granular feed
for: A quick, even feed for vegetable beds and borders before sowing and planting.
how: Scatter it evenly and rake it in, then water. Keep it off wet leaves.
when: A week before sowing or planting, and as a top-up in early summer.

name: Sulphate of potash
for: Flowers and fruit: apples, pears, plums, currants, gooseberries and flowering shrubs. Firmer fruit, sweeter too.
how: Sprinkle it under the branches, as far out as they reach, and water it in.
when: Late winter or early spring, as buds break.
dose: a small handful a square metre

name: Sulphate of ammonia
for: A quick nitrogen boost for leafy crops coming out of winter: spring cabbage, kale and overwintered onions.
how: Sprinkle it thinly between the plants, keeping it off the leaves, and water it in.
when: Early spring, once growth starts. Once is enough.
dose: a small handful a square metre
careful: It makes the soil more acid. Not with lime, and not for beans or peas.

name: Ericaceous feed
for: Plants that need acid soil: blueberries, camellias, rhododendrons, azaleas, pieris and heathers.
how: Dilute it as the bottle says and water it on. Rainwater is best: hard tap water undoes it.
when: Every two weeks from spring to late summer, more often in pots.
dose: as the bottle says, in a can of rainwater

name: Slow-release granules
for: Pots, baskets and window boxes: one feed that lasts the summer.
how: Mix it into the compost when you plant, or push it into the top of the pot.
when: Spring, at potting. It lasts about six months.
dose: a teaspoon for a big pot

name: Wood ash
for: A little potash for fruit bushes, onions, gooseberries and the compost heap.
how: Sprinkle it thinly round plants, or add it to the compost heap a scoop at a time.
when: Late winter and spring, kept dry until then: rain washes the potash out.
homeMade: From a fire or stove burning clean, untreated wood. Not from coal or painted wood. Free.
careful: It makes the soil less acid: not near blueberries or other acid lovers, and not on potatoes (scab).
